title: Comments of the Alaska Center in opposition to the Preliminary Permit Application for the DeepGreen Cook Inlet Subsea-Compute and Infrastructure Hub Project under P-15423.

documents.name: FERC Cook Inlet Comment.pdf
documents.text:
​ O:​
T                ​ ederal Energy Regulatory Commission​
                 F
​FROM:​          ​T​he Alaska Center​
 ​DATE:​          ​November 2, 2026​
  ​RE:​            ​P-15423-000​

​ he​ ​Alaska​ ​Center​ ​is​ ​a​ ​nonprofit​ ​organization​ ​working​ ​to​​engage,​​empower,​​and​​elect​
T
​Alaskans​ ​to​ ​stand​ ​up​ ​for​ ​our​ ​clean​ ​air​ ​and​ ​water,​ ​healthy​ ​communities,​ ​and​ ​a​ ​strong​
 ​democracy.​ ​On​ ​behalf​ ​of​ ​our​ ​members​ ​and​ ​supporters,​ ​we​ ​submit​ ​the​ ​following​
  ​comments.​

​ e​ ​strongly​ ​urge​ ​the​ ​Federal​ ​Energy​ ​Regulatory​ ​Commission​ ​(FERC)​ ​not​ ​to​
W
​approve​ ​DeepGreen’s​ ​initial​ ​permit​ ​to​ ​explore​ ​building​ ​a​ ​sub-sea​ ​data​ ​center​ ​in​
 ​Cook​ ​Inlet.​ ​The​ ​potential​ ​to​ ​irrevocably​ ​harm​ ​some​ ​of​ ​Alaska’s​ ​most​​sensitive​​waters​
  ​and surrounding communities is simply not worth risking for this novel buildout.​

​ eepGreen is proposing to test the new concept of a large-scale, sub-sea data center in​
D
​some of the harshest waters it could select. Cook Inlet’s waters are as ecologically​
 ​important as they are turbulent. Alaskans are very aware that DeepGreen’s data center​
  ​proposal is far from logistically feasible. The likelihood of breakdown, and need for​
   ​constant maintenance resulting from strong currents, silty waters, and extreme​
    ​temperatures makes this choice of location highly perplexing.​

​ he technology proposed for this data center would have very real consequences for​
T
​the Cook Inlet’s marine life and local fisheries. First and foremost - a subsea data center​
 ​will dispel waste heat into a very cold ocean. A 100 MW data center could release about​
  ​876 gigawatt-hours of thermal energy per year if it runs constantly.​

​ aste heat is not directed into a vacuum, it has very real consequences for the​
W
​temperature of the water in the area in which it is expelled. The potential for a​
 ​warm-water plume could affect the behavior and wellbeing of sea life, including notable​
  ​salmon runs in the area.​

​ lans for the cooling system, according to DeepGreen, also include copper-nickel​
P
​cooling fins. Given the high currents native to the area, and high levels of silt, sediment,​
 ​and likely abrasion we need to know how much copper is at risk of entering the​
  ​environment. Even a small amount of copper is deadly to salmon, and could collapse a​
   ​hallmark industry within Alaska’s economy. Many communities, along with native​
 s​ pecies such as bears, wolverines, and wolves count on Cook Inlet salmon as a staple​
 ​food source.​

​ he proposed data center location is also home to Cook Inlet Belugas - one of the most​
T
​endangered species of whale in the world. Cook Inlet Beluga’s must pass through the​
 ​proposed project groups to access feeding and calving grounds. Industrial noise​
  ​pollution already threatens the belugas ability to communicate. Therefore, it is​
   ​paramount that FERC understand to what degree a subsea data center would create​
    ​noise, and how this can be remedied.​

I​n summary, the proposal before FERC is speculative, with high risks and unclear​
 ​benefits to local residents. Analysis shows that this proposal came from an out of state​
  ​company with little knowledge of the region. We strongly suggest FERC deny an initial​
   ​permit to DeepGreen on lack of merit and a failure to understand environmental​
    ​conditions.​

​ hank​ ​you​ ​for​ ​your​ ​attention​ ​on​ ​these​ ​critically​ ​important​​issues,​​and​​how​​they​​impact​
T
​Alaska. We look forward to receiving a detailed response to the above.​

J​ ennifer Hyde​
 ​Federal Engagement Coordinator​
  ​The Alaska Center​
   ​jennifer@akcenter.org​
